title: Hülegü captures Aleppo
summary: Hülegü crossed the Euphrates, besieged Aleppo and took the city; the defenders of the citadel later submitted.
detail: Two years after destroying Baghdad, Hülegü turned on the Ayyubid princes of Syria in the winter of 1259–60. His army, joined by King Hethum I of Cilician Armenia and Prince Bohemond VI of Antioch, surrounded Aleppo, the great fortified city of northern Syria, and bombarded it with mangonels. The lower city fell and was plundered; the governor Turanshah, an elderly son of Saladin, held out in the citadel on its mound for some weeks longer before it too surrendered. The Armenian chronicler Kirakos, writing within a few years, records the siege, the fall of the city and the later submission of the fortress. The fall of Aleppo broke Ayyubid resistance: Hama opened its gates, and the Ayyubid ruler al-Nasir Yusuf abandoned Damascus.
significance: It marked the high point of Mongol power in Syria and brought on the collapse of the Ayyubid principalities, which left Mamluk Egypt as the last organised Muslim power in the region.
uncertaintyNote: Arabic chronicles date the siege to Safar 658 AH (late January 1260) and the citadel's surrender to February; the pack locator does not give the duration, so only the month is shown here. Accounts of the scale of the massacre are rhetorical and are not reproduced.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.62 (Bedrosian trans.)
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World

title: Hülegü leaves a garrison in Syria and withdraws
summary: After Aleppo, Damascus and the other Syrian cities submitted, Hülegü left Kitbuqa with a garrison army in Syria and took his main force back to his winter quarters in Azerbaijan.
detail: With Aleppo fallen, al-Nasir Yusuf fled south and Damascus surrendered without a fight in spring 1260; Kitbuqa, a Nestorian Christian of the Naiman, took charge of it. Mongol detachments raided as far as Gaza. Then Hülegü turned back east, leaving Kitbuqa in Syria with a much reduced army. Why he left is debated. The traditional explanation is that news of the Great Khan Möngke's death and the coming succession struggle drew him east. In a letter of 1262 to Louis IX of France, however, Hülegü himself blamed a lack of fodder and pasture in Syria, and the growing threat from his cousin Berke in the Caucasus was another factor. Whatever the reason, the garrison left behind was too small to hold the country against a determined attack from Egypt.
significance: The withdrawal left Syria to a weak garrison and set up the confrontation at Ain Jalut.
uncertaintyNote: Kirakos records the garrisoning and the return but not the reason. Modern historians (notably Jackson) doubt that Möngke's death was the main cause, as the traditional account claims. Size estimates for Kitbuqa's force vary widely and are not shown. The Christian legend that Kitbuqa entered Damascus with Hethum and Bohemond is not accepted by modern scholars.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.62 (Bedrosian trans.)
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World
Jackson, The Mongols and the West

title: Toluid civil war: Kublai against Ariq Böke
place: Mongolia and the northern Chinese frontier
summary: After Möngke's death, two of his brothers claimed the throne: Kublai was proclaimed at Kaiping and Ariq Böke near Qaraqorum. Four years of war ended with Ariq Böke's surrender in 1264.
detail: Both sides were Toluid Mongols; the atlas follows Kublai, who won. Ariq Böke, regent in the homeland, controlled Qaraqorum and much of the old imperial elite. Kublai held north China. At a partisan assembly at Kaiping he was proclaimed khan on 5 May 1260, taking the Chinese reign title Zhongtong; weeks later Ariq Böke's supporters proclaimed him west of Qaraqorum. Kublai's armies defeated Ariq Böke's allies in Gansu, where the general Alamdar was killed, and Kublai stopped the grain convoys on which the steppe capital depended. In November 1261 Kublai beat Ariq Böke at Shimutu Naoer (Shimultai) on the edge of the Gobi. Ariq Böke then lost the support of Alghu, the Chagatayid khan he had installed, and his coalition fell apart. In August 1264 he came to Kublai's court and submitted. He died in 1266.
significance: The double election ended the united Mongol Empire. Kublai won, but the western khanates never again accepted a Great Khan's authority as they had under Möngke.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi dates the accessions by lunar month (Kublai in the third month, Ariq Böke in the fourth); 5 May 1260 is the usual conversion for Kublai. The site of Shimutu Naoer is not securely identified, so it is not given a marker. The rival kurultais are merged into this event in the research pack.
sources: Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire
Biran, Qaidu and the Rise of the Independent Mongol State in Central Asia
Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6

title: Ain Jalut: the Mamluks defeat Kitbuqa
place: Plain below Mount Tabor (Jezreel Valley), traditional site of Ain Jalut
casualties: Kitbuqa was killed and his army destroyed; reported totals are not reliable.
summary: An Egyptian Mamluk army under Sultan Qutuz advanced into Palestine and defeated and killed Kitbuqa near Mount Tabor, the first decisive defeat of a Mongol army in the Middle East.
detail: The Mamluks of Egypt were slave soldiers, many of them Qipchaq Turks from the steppe the Mongols had conquered. When Hülegü demanded their submission, Sultan Qutuz put the envoys to death and marched north; the Franks of Acre let his army pass and bought supplies from it. Baybars led the vanguard, which made first contact and drew the Mongols on. In the valley below Mount Tabor, at the spring the Arabic sources call Ain Jalut, the armies met on 3 September 1260. The Mongol attack broke one Mamluk wing, but Qutuz rallied his troops and counter-attacked; the Ayyubid prince of Homs, fighting on the Mongol side, deserted. Kitbuqa refused to flee, was captured and killed. Within weeks Damascus and Aleppo were in Mamluk hands, and Baybars had murdered Qutuz and taken the throne.
significance: Ain Jalut ended the idea that the Mongols could not be beaten, fixed the Euphrates as the frontier between the Ilkhanate and the Mamluks, and made the Mamluk Sultanate the leading power of the Islamic world.
uncertaintyNote: The date is from the Arabic sources (25 Ramadan 658). Kirakos places the battle on the plain near Mount Tabor, and the spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa is the traditional site, but it has not been independently fixed, so the atlas shows an area. Army sizes on both sides are chronicle estimates and are not given here.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.62 (Bedrosian trans.)
May, The Mongol Conquests in World History

title: First Battle of Homs

sides.opponent: Ayyubid princes of Homs and Hama with Mamluk troops

summary: A Mongol force sent to recover Syria after Ain Jalut reoccupied Aleppo, then was defeated at Homs on 10 December 1260 by the Ayyubid princes of Homs and Hama and their Mamluk allies.
detail: Hülegü did not accept the loss of Syria. In late 1260 he sent an army back across the Euphrates. It retook Aleppo, where the new Mamluk garrison withdrew, and advanced south. On 10 December 1260 (5 Muharram 659) it met a coalition at Homs led by the Ayyubid princes of Homs and Hama, whom the Mamluks had confirmed in their lands, supported by Mamluk troops from the garrisons. Ibn Wasil of Hama, who wrote soon afterwards and drew on eyewitness reports, describes a Mongol defeat followed by retreat to the east. Later Mamluk writers turned the battle into a story of a small Muslim army beating a much larger Mongol one, and those figures are uncertain. The Mongols fell back across the Euphrates.
significance: It showed that Ain Jalut had not been a fluke and confirmed the Mamluk hold on Syria while Baybars was still establishing himself as sultan.
uncertaintyNote: Troop numbers in Mamluk sources (often 6,000 Mongols against about 1,400 defenders) are not reliable and are not treated as fact here. The exact battlefield near Homs is unknown.

title: Berke–Hülegü war on the Darband–Volga frontier
place: North Caucasus steppe between Darband and the lower Volga
summary: The first full war between two Mongol khanates: Hülegü marched north through the pass at Darband into Golden Horde territory, was defeated in a major battle beyond it and withdrew, and winter campaigns across the frontier went on until Berke's death.
detail: The atlas treats Hülegü, a Toluid, as the protagonist of this Mongol-on-Mongol war. Berke, a Muslim convert, condemned the execution of the caliph at Baghdad, claimed Azerbaijan for the house of Jochi, and blamed Hülegü for the deaths of Jochid princes serving in his army. He also allied with the Mamluks. In the winter of 1262–63 Hülegü forced the Darband pass and plundered Golden Horde camps, then was defeated by Nogai's counter-attack. Kirakos, writing at the time, describes a great battle by the river he calls the Etil (Volga). Rashid al-Din places the rout on the Terek, where the ice broke under the retreating army. Hülegü withdrew through Darband. Abaqa repelled a Golden Horde invasion in 1265, and Berke died in 1266 near Tiflis while trying to cross the Kura.
significance: The war made the Caucasus a permanent frontier between the western khanates and pushed the Golden Horde into a lasting alliance with Mamluk Egypt against the Ilkhanate.
uncertaintyNote: Kirakos (the pack locator) puts the main battle by the Volga; Rashid al-Din puts the January 1263 disaster on the Terek. The atlas shows the frontier region, not a battlefield. Berke's death is dated 1266 or early 1267. The pack window starts in 1261 with the breakdown in relations; the first large campaign came in the winter of 1262-63.
sources: Kirakos Gandzakets’i, History of the Armenians ch.65 (Bedrosian trans.)
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Li Tan's rebellion and the siege of Jinan

sides.opponent: Li Tan, semi-independent warlord of Shandong, allied with the Song

summary: The Shandong warlord Li Tan rebelled and went over to the Song while Kublai was fighting Ariq Böke. He took Jinan, was besieged there for months and was captured and executed when it fell.
detail: Li Tan had inherited a near-independent domain in Shandong from his father and had long played the Mongols and the Song against each other. In early 1262, judging that the civil war had stretched Kublai too thin, he killed the Mongol garrisons, handed coastal towns to the Song, left his base at Yidu and seized Jinan. Kublai's Chinese generals, above all Shi Tianze, surrounded the city with earthworks and starved it out. When Jinan fell in the summer, Li Tan was captured and executed. Worse for the Chinese officials at court, his father-in-law Wang Wentong, one of Kublai's senior ministers, was found to have been in contact with him and was put to death.
significance: The rebellion made Kublai lastingly wary of Chinese advisers and hereditary Chinese warlords. He curbed their autonomy and relied more on Central Asian and Mongol officials.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 5, Shizu benji 世祖本紀, Zhongtong 3 (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Yuan shi 元史, juan 206, Li Tan zhuan 李璮傳; reconciled with Song shi jishi benmo 宋史紀事本末, juan 104, Li Tan zhi na 李璮之納 (Chinese originals; my translation)
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6

title: Nogai's campaign into Byzantine Thrace
summary: Golden Horde forces under Nogai, with Bulgarian support, swept into Byzantine Thrace during a dispute over detained envoys and won the release of the former Seljuk sultan Kaykaus II.
detail: The Seljuk sultan Kaykaus II had fled Anatolia, which was under Mongol control, to Constantinople, where Michael VIII held him while courting Hülegü. Kaykaus had kin and supporters in the Golden Horde, and Golden Horde envoys were also caught up in the dispute. In the winter of 1264–65 Nogai's horsemen, joined by the Bulgarian tsar Constantine Tikh, crossed the Danube into Thrace. According to Pachymeres the emperor, returning from campaign, was nearly caught and escaped only by fleeing across the hills to the coast. The raiders plundered the countryside and took Kaykaus back to the steppe, where he spent the rest of his life in Crimea. Michael later married his illegitimate daughter Euphrosyne to Nogai, and the two remained on working terms for decades.
significance: The campaign established Nogai as an independent power in the Balkans and forced Byzantium to balance between the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
uncertaintyNote: Pachymeres, Gregoras and the Arabic sources (al-Mufaddal) disagree on the chronology; this follows the reconciled 1264–65 window. Later writers repeat the campaign under other dates. Claims of a siege of Constantinople, the route and any tribute paid are not supported and are not shown.
sources: Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Sichuan front: fighting at Diaoyu and a Yuan field administration
summary: In 1265 Yuan forces fought Song troops at Diaoyu Mountain, the fortress where Möngke had died, while Kublai's court set up garrison farms and a field administration to support a long war in Sichuan.
detail: Sichuan was a war of mountain fortresses. In the 1240s the Song had moved towns and garrisons onto flat-topped heights ringed by cliffs and rivers, and Diaoyu, above the meeting of the Jialing and Fu rivers, had held off Möngke in 1259. After the civil war Kublai returned to the problem methodically. The Yuanshi records an engagement at Diaoyu Mountain in February 1265, orders for soldiers to farm land in western Sichuan to feed themselves, and the move of the Qin-Shu field administration to Xingyuan (Hanzhong) to direct operations. The Songshi records continued fighting that year and rewards for defenders at Yunding Mountain and Jintang Gorge. The front hardly moved. Diaoyu held out until 1279, surrendering only after the Song court itself had fallen.
significance: The Sichuan stalemate showed that the Song could not be defeated fortress by fortress, which is why Kublai made the Han River and Xiangyang the main line of attack.
uncertaintyNote: The sources name places and measures but give few commanders or numbers for 1265. The Song context sites at Yunding and Jintang Gorge are not mapped because their positions are uncertain.
sources: Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6
Lorge, War, Politics and Society in Early Modern China

title: Crisis in Tibet: Drigung-aligned opposition suppressed

sides.opponent: Opposition aligned with the Drigung order

opponent: Drigung-aligned leaders (unnamed in the sources used)

summary: The death in 1267 of Chakna Dorje, Kublai's Sakya viceroy in Tibet, set off opposition aligned with the rival Drigung order; by 1268 a force sent by Kublai had put it down.
detail: Kublai governed Tibet through the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism. Its leader Phagpa was his spiritual preceptor, and Phagpa's younger brother Chakna Dorje was appointed to rule Tibet in the khan's name. Rival monastic houses, especially the Drigung, which had ties to Hülegü's branch of the family, resented Sakya supremacy. When Chakna Dorje died in 1267, opposition broke out. Kublai responded with troops, and by 1268 the Sakya order had been restored. That year Yuan officials took a census of Tibet's households and set up relay stations, and a Sakya administrator (dpon-chen) became the chief civil officer. The next year Phagpa presented Kublai with his new script for writing the empire's languages. Larger Drigung conflicts followed in the 1280s, but they are separate episodes.
significance: Suppressing the opposition put Tibet under Yuan–Sakya rule and set the pattern of Tibetan religious leaders working with Mongol military power, which lasted for centuries.
uncertaintyNote: Tibetan and Chinese sources are thin on the 1267–68 events; the commanders of the punitive force and the places involved are not securely named, so the atlas shows only a regional area. The Drigung rebellion of 1285–90 is a separate event and is not merged into this one.
sources: Petech, Central Tibet and the Mongols
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Qaidu's war against Qubilai

sides.opponent: Kaidu's coalition (Ögedeid and Chagatayid princes, with Jochid support)

summary: Kaidu, grandson of Ögedei, refused Kublai's summons, built an anti-Toluid coalition in Central Asia and fought Kublai's armies for the rest of the reign. The war went on after 1294.
detail: Kaidu came from the line of Ögedei that had lost the throne to the Toluids in 1251. From his lands in the Ili and Emil valleys he refused to attend Kublai's court and, with Jochid support, took control of the Chagatayid khanate after Baraq's defeat. His wars were fought on the move: raids into Uighur country and the Tarim oases, clashes on the Mongolian steppe, pressure on Yuan garrisons. Kublai sent princes and his best generals against him, but a mutiny in 1276 wrecked one expedition. In 1289 Kaidu defeated Kublai's grandson Kammala and seized Qaraqorum for a time, and the aged Kublai marched out in person before Bayan took command of the frontier. Rashid al-Din also records Kaidu fighting Abaqa's Ilkhanate. The war did not end with Kublai's death: Kaidu fought his successor until he died of wounds in 1301.
significance: Kaidu's war permanently split Central Asia from the Yuan and showed that even at the height of its power Kublai's empire could not bring the steppe west of Mongolia under control.
uncertaintyNote: The atlas cuts this war off at 1294 for scope, not because it ended. When it began is also debatable: Kaidu's refusal dates from the mid-1260s and open war from about 1268. How long Kaidu held Qaraqorum in 1289, and whether he held it at all, is disputed. The pack labels the span 1260s-1294; the atlas starts it at about 1268.
sources: Biran, Qaidu and the Rise of the Independent Mongol State in Central Asia
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Sieges of Xiangyang and Fancheng
place: Xiangyang and Fancheng, on the Han River, Hubei
summary: For almost five years Yuan forces besieged the twin fortress cities that guarded the Han River route into the Song heartland. Counterweight trebuchets broke Fancheng in early 1273, and Xiangyang surrendered weeks later.
detail: Xiangyang and Fancheng faced each other across the Han, linked by a pontoon bridge. Their walls and river supply lines had defeated earlier Mongol attacks. On the advice of the Song defector Liu Zheng, Aju chose to starve them out rather than storm them. He built forts on the surrounding hills and walls across the valley, and built a river fleet of his own to cut the Han. Song relief convoys broke through at great cost; in 1272 the officers Zhang Shun and Zhang Gui ran supplies in and both were killed. The deadlock ended when two Muslim engineers from the Ilkhanate, Ismail and Ala al-Din, built counterweight trebuchets far more powerful than the traction machines used in China. Their stones smashed Fancheng's defences; the city was stormed and its commanders died. When the machines were turned on Xiangyang, Lü Wenhuan surrendered in 1273 and joined the Yuan.
significance: The fall of Xiangyang opened the Han and the Yangtze to the Yuan and made the conquest of the Southern Song only a matter of time. The trebuchets are the best-documented case of military technology moving across the Mongol Empire.
uncertaintyNote: The start is usually dated to the autumn of 1268, when Aju began the siege works; some accounts start in 1267. Fleet and troop totals in the Yuanshi are not shown. Marco Polo claims that he and his relatives built the trebuchets, but this is false: the siege was over before they reached China.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 162, Li Ting zhuan 李庭傳 and Shi Bi zhuan 史弼傳, Zhiyuan 6-10 (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Song shi jishi benmo 宋史紀事本末, juan 106, Menggu xian Xiangyang 蒙古陷襄陽, Xianchun 9 (Chinese original; my translation)
Franke, 'Siege and Defense of Towns in Medieval China' in Kierman & Fairbank (eds.), Chinese Ways in Warfare
Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 pt. 6
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Baraq invades Khurasan and is defeated by Abaqa
summary: Encouraged by the Talas agreement, the Chagatayid khan Baraq crossed the Oxus into Khurasan and camped near Merv, but his allies deserted and Abaqa's army crushed him.
detail: The atlas treats the Toluid Ilkhan Abaqa as the protagonist of this Mongol-on-Mongol war. At an assembly in the Talas valley, usually dated to 1269, Baraq, Kaidu and envoys of the Golden Horde divided the revenues of Transoxiana and gave Baraq licence to seek new lands in Ilkhanid Khurasan. In 1270 he crossed the Oxus and advanced to Merv. Rashid al-Din describes princes sent by Kaidu deserting him during the campaign, and his army fraying as it plundered. Abaqa marched east from Azerbaijan and defeated him; the sources place the decisive battle near Herat that summer. Baraq, who had been partly paralysed in a riding accident, escaped across the Oxus but his authority collapsed. He died in 1271, and Kaidu became the real master of the Chagatayid lands.
significance: The defeat secured the Ilkhanate's eastern frontier for a generation and delivered the Chagatai Khanate into Kaidu's hands.
uncertaintyNote: Rashid al-Din dates the decisive battle to July 1270 near Herat, but the pack locator supports only the campaign and a Merv marker, so no battlefield is plotted. Army sizes are not reliable. The date of the Talas assembly (1267, 1269 or later) is disputed; Biran argues for 1269.
sources: Biran, Qaidu and the Rise of the Independent Mongol State in Central Asia
Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World

title: Sambyeolcho revolt: Ganghwa, Jindo and Jeju

sides.mongol: Yuan (Kublai) with the Goryeo royal government

summary: When the Goryeo court made peace with the Mongols and returned to the mainland, the Sambyeolcho elite troops rebelled on Ganghwa Island, set up a rival regime on Jindo and, after its fall, held out on Jeju until joint Yuan–Goryeo forces crushed them in 1273.
detail: For nearly forty years the Goryeo court had resisted the Mongols from Ganghwa Island. In 1270 King Wonjong, backed by Kublai, ended military rule and ordered the court back to Kaesong. The Sambyeolcho, the military regime's elite 'Three Patrols', refused. Under Bae Jung-son they proclaimed a rival king, loaded ships with people and treasure and sailed south to Jindo, where they built a fortress and raided the southern coasts. In 1271 a combined Yuan–Goryeo force under Hindu, Hong Dagu and Kim Bang-gyeong stormed Jindo. Kim Tong-jeong escaped with the survivors to Jeju (Tamna), which he fortified. In 1273 the allies landed there and destroyed the last rebels. The Yuan then set up a horse-breeding station and garrison on Jeju.
significance: Crushing the revolt tied Goryeo firmly to the Yuan and freed Korean shipyards and troops for the invasion of Japan the following year.
uncertaintyNote: The Goryeosa and the Yuanshi agree on the sequence. Sea routes between the three stages are not reconstructed and are not drawn. The revolt is treated as a series of separate stages, not one continuous campaign. The pack row is labelled 1269-1273; the revolt itself broke out in the sixth lunar month of 1270, the date the atlas uses.
sources: Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: First invasion of Japan (Bun'ei campaign)
summary: After overrunning Tsushima and Iki, a Yuan–Korean fleet landed at Hakata Bay and fought the Kyushu warriors for a day, burning Hakata, then re-embarked and withdrew.
detail: Kublai's letters demanding submission had gone unanswered since 1268. In November 1274 a fleet of Korean-built ships sailed from southern Korea, wiped out the small garrisons of Tsushima and Iki, and landed around Hakata Bay. The invaders fought in close formations to the sound of drums and gongs, shooting short bows in volleys and throwing exploding ceramic bombs. The Mongol Invasion Scrolls, commissioned by the warrior Takezaki Suenaga to record his service, show one bursting beside his wounded horse. The Japanese warriors fell back inland towards the old fortifications near Dazaifu, and the Hakozaki shrine burned. But the invaders' deputy commander Liu Fuxiang had been wounded, arrows were running short, and that night the commanders decided to leave. The Goryeosa records heavy losses at sea on the return voyage.
significance: The invasion showed that Japan could be struck but not easily held, and led the Kamakura shogunate to build a stone wall around Hakata Bay against a second attack.
uncertaintyNote: The Japanese lunar date (Bun'ei 11, 10th month, 20th day) is usually converted to 19–20 November 1274. Whether a storm drove the fleet off or it withdrew by plan and was caught by bad weather at sea is disputed; Conlan argues the withdrawal was a decision made in the face of resistance. Fleet and army totals from the Yuanshi and Goryeosa are not given here.
sources: Takezaki Suenaga, Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba / Scrolls of the Mongol Invasions (eyewitness-commissioned record; Princeton Digital project, annotated scrolls)
Conlan, In Little Need of Divine Intervention

title: Battle of Dingjiazhou
place: Dingjiazhou reach of the Yangtze, between Chizhou and Wuhu
summary: The chief minister Jia Sidao led the Song's largest remaining army and fleet up the Yangtze to stop Bayan. At Dingjiazhou it broke under attack, and Jia fled towards Yangzhou.
detail: Bayan had come down the Han from Xiangyang in autumn 1274 and forced a crossing of the Yangtze near Hankou in January 1275. The Song answered with everything it had left. Jia Sidao, the dominant minister of the late Song, took personal command and moved upriver. At Dingjiazhou, where the river narrows below Chizhou, the armies met in the second lunar month of 1275. The Yuan attacked with artillery from the banks, cavalry along both shores and ships on the river. Sun Huchen's vanguard wavered, Xia Gui withdrew his fleet without fighting, and panic swept the crowded Song boats. Jia Sidao fled towards Yangzhou. The court dismissed him, and later that year he was murdered by the officer escorting him into exile. Jiankang (Nanjing) and the towns of the lower Yangtze soon opened their gates.
significance: Dingjiazhou destroyed the Song's last great field army and opened the road to the capital, Lin'an.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi gives only the lunar month (Zhiyuan 12, second month, i.e. March 1275). Traditional Song army and fleet totals come from a historiography that made Jia Sidao a scapegoat and are not shown. The exact position of the battle on the river is not fixed.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 8, Shizu benji 世祖本紀, Zhiyuan 12 second month (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Yuan shi 元史, juan 131, Mangwutai zhuan 忙兀台傳 and Wanzhedu zhuan 完者都傳; Song shi 宋史, juan 474, Jia Sidao zhuan 賈似道傳 (Chinese originals; my translation)
Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6

title: Mutiny of the princes: Nomoghan seized
place: Western steppe frontier of the Yuan, towards the Irtysh

sides.opponent: Mutinous Toluid princes (Shiregi, Toq Temür), handing captives to the Golden Horde and Kaidu

summary: Princes serving in the army Kublai had sent against Kaidu mutinied, seized his son Nomoghan and the minister Hantum in a night raid, handed them over to the Golden Horde and Kaidu, and then fought Kublai's loyal troops.
detail: Kublai had sent his son Nomoghan west with an army of princes to contain Kaidu. Among them were Shiregi, son of Möngke, and other descendants of Tolui who resented Kublai's Chinese-style rule and felt passed over. In 1276 they struck. Rashid al-Din describes a night raid in which Nomoghan, his brother Kököchü and the minister Hantum (Antong) were seized. Nomoghan was sent to the Golden Horde khan Möngke Temür, and Hantum to Kaidu. The mutineers then turned on Kublai's loyal forces. Loyalist armies defeated them. Rashid al-Din records a clash on the banks of the Irtysh, and the Chinese sources credit Bayan, recalled from his triumph in the south, with a victory in Mongolia in 1277. The rebels fell out among themselves. Nomoghan was not released until 1284.
significance: The mutiny showed that some of Kublai's closest relatives rejected his rule, and it stalled Yuan operations in Central Asia, leaving the field open to Kaidu.
uncertaintyNote: The event is often placed at Almaliq, but the pack locator (Rashid al-Din) does not support that, so no seizure site is plotted. How far Kaidu was involved in the plot is debated; Biran argues he benefited from it rather than planned it.
sources: Biran, Qaidu and the Rise of the Independent Mongol State in Central Asia
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Surrender of Lin'an, the Song capital

markers.name: Gaoting Mountain (Yuan camp on the northern approach)

summary: With Bayan's army camped at Gaoting Mountain, the Song court sent out its seal and a memorial of surrender. Yuan officials took over the capital, the largest city in the world, without a battle.
detail: Lin'an, perhaps the largest city in the world, was the commercial and cultural centre of Song China. By early 1276 Bayan's army was camped at Gaoting Mountain on its northern approach, and many senior officials had fled. The Grand Empress Dowager Xie, ruling for the five-year-old Emperor Gong, sent out the imperial seal and a memorial of surrender. Wen Tianxiang, sent to negotiate, argued so defiantly with Bayan that he was detained, though he later escaped to fight on. Bayan kept his troops out of the city, sealed the treasuries and archives, and sent the young emperor and the court north to Kublai, who treated them honourably. Two younger princes had already been smuggled south to carry on the dynasty.
significance: The surrender of the capital effectively ended the Southern Song as a state and gave Kublai the richest region of China almost undamaged.
uncertaintyNote: Sources give slightly different dates in the first and second lunar months of Zhiyuan 13 (February–March 1276) for the handing over of the seal and Bayan's entry.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 9, Shizu benji 世祖本紀, Zhiyuan 13 first-second months (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Yuan shi 元史, juan 127, Bayan zhuan 伯顏傳; Song shi jishi benmo 宋史紀事本末, juan 107, Yuan Bayan ru Linan 元伯顏入臨安 (Chinese originals; my translation)
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Yuan–Burmese frontier battle (Ngasaunggyan)
place: Yunnan–Burma frontier, between Nandian and Tengyue/Yongchang
summary: A Burmese army with war elephants attacked A He, a frontier chief under Yuan protection. Yuan troops marched out from Nandian, beat it beside a river, pursued it towards a narrow mountain pass and returned.
detail: The Pagan kingdom (Mian to the Chinese) had refused Kublai's demands for tribute and held his envoys. In spring 1277 a Burmese army moved against A He, a frontier chief who had submitted to the Yuan. The Yunnan garrison marched from Nandian and met it near a river. The Yuanshi describes the Burmese army with elephants and horses, and a Yuan victory followed by pursuit towards a narrow pass. Marco Polo's much-quoted account, which he heard at second hand, adds the famous detail that the Mongol horses panicked at the elephants, so the riders dismounted, tied them among the trees and shot at the elephants until they stampeded back through their own army. Later that year Nasir al-Din led a raid further into Burma before the heat forced him back.
significance: It opened a decade of Yuan pressure on Burma that ended with the collapse of the Pagan kingdom.
uncertaintyNote: The Burmese chronicle name Ngasaunggyan is traditional; the Yuanshi does not fix the river or the pass precisely, so an area is shown. The Yuanshi's figures for the Burmese army and elephants are almost certainly inflated and are not shown. Polo's tactical account is vivid but unconfirmed. The Yuanshi dates the attack to the third lunar month of Zhiyuan 14, which fell in about April 1277 in the Western calendar. The pack row gives it as March.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 210, Mian 緬 entry, Zhiyuan 14 third-month account (Chinese Text Project aligned text/translation)
Aung-Thwin, Myth and History in the Historiography of Early Burma

title: Battle of Yamen (Yashan): the end of the Song
place: Yashan (Yamen) estuary, Xinhui, Pearl River delta
summary: The Yuan fleet destroyed the last Song fleet in the Yashan estuary. The minister Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea holding the seven-year-old emperor Zhao Bing, and the Song dynasty ended.
detail: After Lin'an fell, loyalists crowned two boy princes in turn and retreated down the south coast. By early 1279 the court was anchored at Yashan, a sheltered bay in the Pearl River delta. Zhang Shijie chained his ships into a great floating fortress. The Yuan commander Zhang Hongfan, himself a northern Chinese, came south by sea from Yangzhou while Li Heng came down from Guangzhou. They cut the Song fleet off from fresh water and firewood, so that its crews drank seawater and fell sick. On 19 March the Yuan attacked from north and south, using the tides. As the Song line broke, Lu Xiufu took Zhao Bing in his arms and leapt into the sea. The captured loyalist Wen Tianxiang watched from a Yuan ship. Zhang Shijie broke out, but drowned in a storm days later.
significance: Yashan ended the Song dynasty and completed the Mongol conquest of China, making Kublai the first non-Chinese ruler of the whole country.
uncertaintyNote: The date (Xiangxing 2, second month, sixth day) is well established. The traditional figures of over a thousand Song ships and a hundred thousand dead come from loyalist tradition and are not shown here.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 129, Li Heng zhuan 李恒傳, Zhiyuan 16 second month (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Song shi 宋史, juan 451, Lu Xiufu zhuan 陸秀夫傳; Song shi jishi benmo 宋史紀事本末, juan 108, Er wang zhi li 二王之立 (Chinese originals; my translation)
Lo Jung-pang, China as a Sea Power 1127–1368

title: Second invasion of Japan (Kōan campaign) and the kamikaze
place: Northern Kyushu: Hakata Bay to Imari Bay

sides.mongol: Yuan (Kublai) with Goryeo: Eastern Route and Jiangnan armies

summary: A second, far larger invasion found Hakata Bay walled off and fought for weeks on islands and at sea off northern Kyushu. In mid-August a typhoon wrecked the fleet anchored off Takashima, and the invasion collapsed.
detail: Since 1276 the shogunate had built a stone wall around Hakata Bay. When the Eastern Route Army from Korea arrived in June 1281, it could not land in force. It seized Shikanoshima island, and for days Japanese warriors attacked at night in small boats, boarding enemy ships to fight hand to hand. Kōno Michiari famously used his fallen mast as a ladder to climb aboard. The main Jiangnan army, largely made up of surrendered Song soldiers, sailed late from Qingyuan (Ningbo) and joined the Eastern Route Army off Hirado and Takashima at the mouth of Imari Bay. On the night of 15–16 August a typhoon struck the crowded anchorage and smashed much of the fleet. Commanders took the soundest ships home, and Japanese troops killed or captured the men left stranded on Takashima. Wrecks found in Imari Bay since 2011 are still being studied.
significance: The disaster ended Kublai's attempts on Japan. It became the source of the 'divine wind' (kamikaze) legend, which later became central to Japanese nationalism.
uncertaintyNote: Weeks of Japanese resistance and the invaders' supply and disease problems came before the storm, so the typhoon is not treated as the only cause. The Yuanshi's figures (about 4,400 ships and 140,000 men) are doubted by Conlan and Delgado and are not shown. Delgado's view that the wrecks show poorly built ships is debated. Dates convert from the Japanese lunar calendar (the typhoon struck on the first day of the intercalary seventh month of Kōan 4). The fighting at Shikanoshima (Hakata Bay) and the typhoon at Takashima (Imari Bay) are described in the text but not given pins, because the pack permits only a regional area.
sources: Takezaki Suenaga, Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba / Scrolls of the Mongol Invasions (eyewitness-commissioned record; Princeton Digital project, annotated scrolls)
Conlan, In Little Need of Divine Intervention

title: Second Battle of Homs (between Hama and Homs)

sides.mongol: Ilkhanate with Georgian and Armenian allies

mongol: King Leo II of Cilician Armenia

summary: The largest Ilkhanid invasion of Syria since 1260 met Sultan Qalawun's army between Hama and Homs. The Mongol right wing won its fight, but the centre and left gave way, and the whole army withdrew.
detail: Abaqa sent his brother Möngke Temür into Syria with a large army that included Georgian and Armenian troops under King Leo II, while he himself besieged al-Rahba on the Euphrates. Qalawun, who had seized the throne from Baybars' sons, met them at the end of October. Bar Hebraeus, a Syriac churchman living under the Ilkhans, describes a battle of uneven fortunes. The Mongol right wing broke the Mamluk left and pursued it far from the field, but the Ilkhanid centre and left withdrew, and when the victorious right wing returned it too retired. Mamluk sources add that Möngke Temür was wounded, which may explain why the centre gave way. The retreating army suffered heavily crossing back to the Euphrates.
significance: It confirmed the Mamluk hold on Syria for another generation and ended Abaqa's hopes of a joint campaign with the Franks.
uncertaintyNote: Bar Hebraeus dates the battle to 30 October; Mamluk sources give 14 Rajab 680 (29 October 1281). Army sizes, casualty figures and tactical detail differ between the sources and are not shown. The atlas uses the Mamluk date; the pack locator, Bar Hebraeus, gives 30 October.

title: Yuan invasion of Champa
place: Champa coast around Vijaya (near modern Quy Nhơn)
summary: A Yuan seaborne force under Sogetu landed on the Champa coast in late 1282, stormed the Cham wooden fort in January 1283 and occupied the capital, but faced guerrilla resistance inland and withdrew in March 1284.
detail: Champa, on the central coast of what is now Vietnam, had accepted nominal Yuan overlordship and then held Kublai's envoys. Sogetu, governor of Guangzhou, sailed from there and landed on the Champa coast in late 1282. The Chams had built a long wooden stockade armed with catapults. In January 1283 Sogetu stormed it in a combined night and dawn assault and occupied the capital, Vijaya. The elderly king Indravarman V and his son Harijit withdrew into the hills, sent false offers of submission and ambushed Yuan columns. Reinforcements were slow, and Đại Việt refused the Yuan passage for an overland supply route. In March 1284 Sogetu pulled out. In 1285 he marched north from Champa into Đại Việt, where he was killed.
significance: Champa's resistance, and Đại Việt's refusal to let the Yuan pass, led directly to Kublai's invasions of Vietnam.
uncertaintyNote: Dates follow the Yuanshi (landing November 1282, fort taken January 1283, withdrawal March 1284). The landing beach, the fort's position and the routes inland are not reconstructed. Yuan troop numbers are not shown. The pack row is labelled 1284-1285 but its reconciled id and reasoning give 1282-1284; the atlas follows 1282-1284, and Sogetu’s 1285 march north belongs to the Đại Việt invasion. The months are the pack’s readings of the Yuanshi. If they are lunar months, each Western date falls three to five weeks later.
sources: Coedès, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Second invasion of Đại Việt
summary: Kublai's son Toghon broke through the northern passes and took Thăng Long while the Trần court withdrew. As heat, disease and hunger weakened the invaders, the Vietnamese counter-attacked and drove them out.
detail: When the Trần refused Sogetu passage to Champa, Kublai sent Toghon south from Guangxi in early 1285. His cavalry forced the frontier passes, defeated Trần Hưng Đạo and occupied the empty capital, Thăng Long, while Sogetu pushed north from Champa. The Trần emperors retreated by river and sea, and some princes went over to the Yuan. Trần Hưng Đạo avoided pitched battles, removed food stores and waited. By May the Yuan army was hungry and sick. The Vietnamese counter-attacked: Trần Quang Khải won at Chương Dương and retook the capital, and Sogetu, trying to join Toghon, was killed at Tây Kết. Toghon retreated north, harried through the hills; Li Heng, a veteran of Yamen, died of a poisoned arrow. Vietnamese tradition says Toghon escaped hidden in a bronze tube.
significance: The rout of 1285 was among the Yuan's worst defeats and became a founding story of Vietnamese national history.
uncertaintyNote: The Vietnamese annals and the Yuanshi agree on the course of events but not on numbers, which are not shown. The positions of Chương Dương and Tây Kết are approximate. The bronze tube story and the tradition of soldiers tattooing 'Kill the Tatars' on their arms come from Vietnamese tradition. 1283–84 is treated as part of the Champa war. The pack row is labelled 1283-1285, but its reasoning limits the direct invasion to 1285, which the atlas follows.
sources: Lê Tắc, An Nam chí lược
Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times

title: Hàm Tử: the Vietnamese counter-offensive begins
place: Hàm Tử gate on the Red River (Khoái Châu, Hưng Yên)
summary: In April 1285 Trần forces attacked the Yuan at Hàm Tử on the Red River, the first major victory of the counter-offensive that retook the capital and Chương Dương the following month.
detail: By spring 1285 the Yuan held the Red River delta's cities but not its countryside. Sogetu's army from Champa was working north to join Toghon, and the Yuan forces were stretched along the rivers. At the Hàm Tử crossing, according to the Vietnamese annals, Trần Nhật Duật led an attack that routed a Yuan force. The annals note that he was joined by Song refugees who had fled the Yuan conquest of China, fighting in their own dress. The victory raised Vietnamese morale and opened a series of blows: in May Trần Quang Khải attacked at Chương Dương and retook the capital, and in June Sogetu was killed at Tây Kết.
significance: Hàm Tử marked the turning point from Vietnamese retreat to counter-offensive in 1285, though it was one blow among several rather than the single cause of the Yuan withdrawal.
uncertaintyNote: The Vietnamese annals are the main source for the engagement itself; the Yuanshi records the wider resistance and withdrawal. The exact battlefield and the forces involved are not known.
sources: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese

title: Yuan campaign to Pagan
summary: A Yuan army from Yunnan advanced down into Burma and, according to the Yuanshi, reached Pagan. The dynastic history then records losses and a settlement under which Burma paid tribute.
detail: Yuan forces had stormed the Burmese frontier fort at Kaungsin in 1283, and King Narathihapate abandoned Pagan for the south, earning the name 'the king who fled from the Chinese'. He agreed to submit, but in 1287 he was poisoned by his son Thihathu at Prome. That year an army under Kublai's grandson Yesün Temür marched south from Yunnan. The Yuanshi says it reached Pugan (Pagan) in the 24th year of Zhiyuan, and that it suffered heavy losses before a tributary settlement was reached. The royal house of Pagan never recovered. Power passed to three Shan brothers based at Myinsaing, who accepted Yuan overlordship and later fought off another Yuan army in 1300–01.
significance: The campaign coincided with the end of the Pagan kingdom, which had united the Irrawaddy valley for two and a half centuries, and began a long period of political division in Burma.
uncertaintyNote: Older histories, following Burmese chronicles, say the Mongols sacked Pagan. Than Tun and Aung-Thwin argue they never reached the city and that Pagan declined for internal reasons. The Yuanshi's claim that Burma was thereby pacified, and its loss figures, are not treated as fact here.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 210, Mian 緬 entry, Zhiyuan 23-24 account (Chinese Text Project aligned text/translation)
Aung-Thwin, Myth and History in the Historiography of Early Burma
Coedès, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia

title: Nayan's rebellion crushed by Kublai

sides.opponent: Nayan and the eastern princes (descendants of Chinggis Khan's brothers), in league with Kaidu

summary: Nayan, head of the eastern princely houses, rebelled in 1287 in league with Kaidu. The 72-year-old Kublai led the army in person, defeated and captured him, and his forces fought on against the remaining rebels into 1288.
detail: The eastern princes, descended from Chinggis Khan's brothers, ruled their own peoples in Manchuria and resented Kublai's taxes and officials. In 1287 Nayan, a Nestorian Christian of the Otchigin line, rose in revolt, expecting Kaidu to attack from the west. Kublai, old and suffering from gout, moved fast. He sent Bayan to hold Qaraqorum against Kaidu and marched north-east himself. Marco Polo claims the khan directed the battle from a wooden tower carried by four elephants, and that crosses flew on Nayan's banners. Nayan was defeated and captured. As a Chinggisid whose blood could not be shed, he was wrapped in felt and beaten to death. Yuan forces spent 1288 hunting down his allies, and the princes Qadan and Shiktür resisted for several more years.
significance: Kublai's last great personal campaign kept Manchuria and the eastern steppe from joining Kaidu and held the Yuan state together.
uncertaintyNote: The battlefield is not identified. Polo's army totals (hundreds of thousands) and his elephant-tower account are colourful but unconfirmed; the Yuanshi is terser and gives no reliable totals.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 133, Tachu zhuan 塔出傳 and related campaign biographies (Chinese original; my translation for atlas wording)
Yuan shi jishi benmo 元史紀事本末, juan 2, Beibian zhuwang zhi luan 北邊諸王之亂, Zhiyuan 24-25 (Chinese original chronological reconciliation; my translation)
Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire

title: Third invasion of Đại Việt and the Battle of Bạch Đằng
place: Northern Đại Việt, from the Red River delta to the Bạch Đằng estuary
summary: Toghon invaded again in late 1287, but the grain fleet never reached him. As the Yuan fleet retreated down the Bạch Đằng in April 1288, it was caught on iron-tipped stakes planted in the riverbed and destroyed.
detail: Kublai sent Toghon back with a larger army and a war fleet under Omar, backed by a separate grain convoy. The warships pushed through, but Trần Khánh Dư caught the slower grain fleet among the islands off Vân Đồn, and the supplies were lost. Toghon reoccupied an empty Thăng Long and found nothing to eat. In spring 1288 he decided to withdraw overland while Omar's fleet went down the Bạch Đằng River to the sea. Trần Hưng Đạo copied a trick used on the same river in 938: his men drove iron-tipped wooden stakes into the riverbed, hidden at high tide. Small boats lured the Yuan fleet in at high water and then retreated. As the tide fell, the ships stuck fast on the stakes and were attacked with fire and from both banks. Omar and Fan Yi were captured. Toghon fought his way back to China.
significance: Bạch Đằng ended Kublai's attempts to conquer Đại Việt and became the defining symbol of Vietnamese resistance to invasion from the north.
uncertaintyNote: The Vietnamese annals date Bạch Đằng to the 8th day of the 3rd lunar month (9 April 1288). The exact stake field, fleet sizes and casualty figures are not reconstructed. Stakes excavated at several sites along the river may come from this battle or from earlier ones.
sources: Lê Tắc, An Nam chí lược
Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese
Lo Jung-pang, China as a Sea Power 1127–1368

title: Yuan expedition to Java and the founding of Majapahit
place: East Java: the Tuban coast and the Brantas river valley

sides.opponent: Kediri (Jayakatwang), then Raden Wijaya of Majapahit

summary: A Yuan fleet sailed in late 1292 to punish Java for insulting Kublai's envoy. It allied with Raden Wijaya to destroy the Kediri ruler Jayakatwang, then was attacked by Wijaya and withdrew. Wijaya went on to found Majapahit.
detail: In 1289 King Kertanegara of Singhasari had Kublai's envoy disfigured and sent back. Kublai ordered a punitive expedition, which sailed from Quanzhou in late 1292. By the time it arrived, Kertanegara had been killed by his vassal Jayakatwang of Kediri. Kertanegara's son-in-law, Raden Wijaya, who had set up a base at a new settlement called Majapahit, offered to submit if the Yuan helped him against Jayakatwang. The Yuan army landed, advanced by water and land up the Brantas river and, with Wijaya's troops, took Jayakatwang's capital, Daha. Wijaya then asked to go home to prepare his tribute. He killed his Yuan escort and attacked the army on its way back to the coast. The commanders sailed for home with plunder and prisoners. Wijaya was crowned king of Majapahit later in 1293.
significance: The expedition was the Yuan's furthest military reach by sea, and it unintentionally helped found Majapahit, which became the leading state of island Southeast Asia in the fourteenth century.
uncertaintyNote: The Yuanshi dates the withdrawal to the 4th lunar month of Zhiyuan 30 (late May 1293). Its force and casualty figures are not shown. Javanese texts (Pararaton, Nagarakretagama) tell the story from Wijaya's side and differ over who deceived whom. Wijaya's coronation is usually dated to November 1293.
sources: Yuan shi 元史, juan 210, Jiawa 爪哇 entry (Chinese Text Project aligned text/translation)
Coedès, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia
Lo Jung-pang, China as a Sea Power 1127–1368

title: Death of Kublai Khan; Temür succeeds
summary: Kublai died in the Zitan Hall of his palace at Dadu in February 1294, aged 78, after 34 years on the throne. His grandson Temür was enthroned at Shangdu that spring.
detail: Kublai's last years were overshadowed by the deaths of his favourite wife Chabi in 1281 and of his chosen heir Zhenjin in 1285, and by failures in Japan, Vietnam and Java. He drank heavily, grew very heavy and suffered from gout. He died in the Zitan Hall of the palace at Dadu in the first lunar month of 1294 (18 February). The succession was settled at an assembly at Shangdu, where Zhenjin's son Temür was enthroned in the fourth month, with Bayan's firm support. Kublai's body was taken north for burial at an unmarked site in the Mongol homeland, as his ancestors had been. He left a Chinese dynasty and a reputation across Eurasia, but the Mongol world was now divided into independent khanates.
significance: Kublai's death closes the atlas and the age of Mongol expansion: his successors made peace with the other khanates in 1304 and never launched another overseas conquest.
uncertaintyNote: The story that Bayan silenced other claimants at the Shangdu assembly with his hand on his sword is a later tradition. The burial site is unknown. The atlas ends at this boundary, but some wars, such as Kaidu's, continued.
sources: Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times
Franke & Twitchett (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 6
